video_title: Christian Mueller-Glissmann on Bonds, AI CapEx, and 60/40 | U Got Options with Cem Karsan
gist: Goldman's Christian Mueller-Glissmann and Cem Karsan debate whether the AI capex boom is an earnings or valuation bubble, how the bond selloff is the speed limit on equities, and why cheap equity/FX volatility, gold and real assets are preferred hedges. Karsan adds a forceful debasement-within-a-year, government-backed-capex thesis.

themes.theme: AI capex boom and the bond speed limit

insights.claim: The 2026 macro regime defied start-of-year expectations: instead of a goldilocks of inflation relief and policy help, an enormous AI capex boom re-accelerated the business cycle to mid-cycle and re-levered the private sector, which had not looked late-cycle at end-2025.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann (Goldman Sachs)
insights.so_what: Growth is nominal and capex-led, so bonds and equities are repricing off a different regime than consensus assumed.

insights.claim: The AI-capex nominal growth acceleration is bullish for equity earnings but bearish for bonds; inflation was driven more by the Middle East war and energy prices than by AI capex itself, so bonds are still searching for a new equilibrium.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann (Goldman Sachs)
insights.so_what: Energy-led inflation plus capex demand keeps long yields under upward pressure even as equity earnings tailwinds fade.

insights.claim: Equities have begun consolidating because the speed of the bond selloff is coinciding with moderating earnings tailwinds that were enormous in the first half of the year; rates headwinds now bite, especially in parts of the market without earnings support.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann (Goldman Sachs)
insights.so_what: The bond market acts as the speed limit on equities once the earnings offset weakens.

insights.claim: The equity reaction to rising yields depends on level, speed and source: the old 5% worry level is a moving target, a rise of more than two standard deviations over three months signals indigestion (the 10-year was past that at roughly 5.1-5.2%), and growth-driven rises are digested better than policy-driven real-yield rises.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann (Goldman Sachs)
insights.so_what: Gives a checklist to judge whether a bond selloff will break equities; currently speed and source are unfavourable.

insights.claim: Rate damage is already visible under the surface: small and mid caps, real estate, home builders, rate-sensitive areas and selective financials are under pressure from higher bond yields.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann (Goldman Sachs)
insights.so_what: Index strength masks rate-driven damage; the pain is concentrated in rate-sensitive sectors.

insights.claim: Growth news flow has been more muted since summer, with consumer-related macro data weakening, so the upcoming Q3 earnings season is the key test of whether AI capex plus visible monetization can let equities digest higher yields.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann (Goldman Sachs)
insights.so_what: Q3 hyperscaler commentary on monetization is the near-term catalyst for the equity-versus-bond tension.

insights.claim: Equity consolidation and higher volatility could stabilize bond yields and temporarily restore equity-bond diversification, though Mueller-Glissmann is still not in the camp that 60/40 will return to its pre-COVID form.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann (Goldman Sachs)
insights.so_what: A short-term friendlier stock-bond correlation is possible, but it is not a structural return of 60/40.
insights.quote: I'm still not in the camp that 6040 portfolios will come back and be what they were before co

insights.claim: Central banks find it hard to step off the pedal on tightening because long-dated yields could unanchor too quickly and create negative feedback loops to equities and the economy.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann (Goldman Sachs)
insights.so_what: Policy relief is constrained, which keeps real yields pressure on risk assets.

insights.claim: Goldman's view is that markets are not in a valuation bubble but are somewhat in an earnings bubble in parts of the market; a valuation bubble can burst quickly whereas an earnings bubble can take a long time to deflate.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann (Goldman Sachs)
insights.so_what: Argues for a slow grind or dispersion rather than a crash, shaping hedging toward convexity rather than shorts.
insights.quote: We are more likely to be a bit in an earnings bubble, at least in some of these parts of the market.

insights.claim: Valuations have already de-rated: the S&P 500 12-month forward P/E fell from about 23x at the start of the year to about 19x, and the MSCI world tech complex forward P/E is down about 15% year to date, showing the market is discounting cyclical AI earnings.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann (Goldman Sachs)
insights.so_what: Some skepticism is already priced, limiting multiple downside absent an earnings miss.

insights.claim: Data-center construction and compute contracts are unusually long-dated, giving more earnings visibility than normal, and near-term compute demand is expected to stay high as workloads shift from frontier-model development to applications.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann (Goldman Sachs)
insights.so_what: Explains why investors are not yet worried about capex cyclicality.

insights.claim: The Shiller P/E (in the 40s, near tech-bubble levels) overstates the problem versus the forward P/E because earnings have risen well above the 10-year average since COVID; S&P 500 return on equity is about 24% versus below 20% five years ago, and more than double late-1990s levels.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann (Goldman Sachs)
insights.so_what: The valuation debate hinges on whether the higher ROE is structural or cyclical.

insights.claim: Hyperscalers' free cash flow is falling out of bed and turning negative even as they are the main contributors to earnings growth, funded by increasing debt; Karsan argues earnings and cash flow are normally correlated and now are far apart.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Earnings quality is weak; the earnings story depends on continued external financing.

insights.claim: Karsan argues earnings have mean-reverted well beyond the mean in past bubbles: earnings are about 50% above the roughly 6% real long-run trend, and tailwinds such as lower tax rates are unlikely to repeat and could reverse with populism.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Supports the bear case that structural-looking margins are cyclical or policy-driven.
insights.quote: historically we actually see more mean reversion

insights.claim: Mueller-Glissmann concedes the AI-capex earnings tailwind is peaking (the second derivative turns less favourable) and that some mean reversion in earnings is coming, but believes part of the last five years of earnings gains (platform companies, cloud) will stick and that the truth is in the middle.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann (Goldman Sachs)
insights.so_what: Expect a partial, gradual earnings give-back rather than a full reset.

insights.claim: Tech is currently harvesting roughly 30% annualized earnings growth, so flat prices imply a 30% de-rating; large downside in tech requires the earnings second derivative to roll over first.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann (Goldman Sachs)
insights.so_what: Downside volatility needs an earnings catalyst, so watch the earnings season for the inflection.

themes.theme: AI productivity J-curve and monetization gap

insights.claim: Every technology revolution moves from an investment phase to an application and adoption phase with a J-curve; AI is early on the curve, with productivity benefits not yet visible in earnings or macro data though Goldman's macro team still sees material productivity gains over the next decade.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann (Goldman Sachs)
insights.so_what: Near-term earnings must come from capex beneficiaries while real productivity payoff is years out.

insights.claim: The market is entering a less tangible phase in which it must assess application success and winners versus losers, implying more dispersion within tech and across the economy.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann (Goldman Sachs)
insights.so_what: Stock-picking and dispersion strategies become more relevant than beta.

insights.claim: Goldman's US strategy team found S&P 500 companies spend only about 0.1% of cost of goods sold on AI tokens and subscriptions, implying a large gap between current spend and monetization potential that must be bridged.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann (Goldman Sachs)
insights.so_what: Monetization must scale substantially to justify the capex; the shortfall is a risk if left too long.

insights.claim: If hyperscalers fail to show AI monetization in Q3, negative free cash flow yields and future depreciation headwinds must be reflected in lower valuations as profitability falls.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann (Goldman Sachs)
insights.so_what: Q3 monetization disclosures are a binary-ish catalyst for AI complex valuations.

insights.claim: Karsan argues markets now drive the economy: roughly $300 trillion of global equities collateralized off S&P 500 levels means April-May's 20% rally added about $50 trillion of collateral, versus about $10 trillion of Fed QE after COVID, feeding capex and then earnings reflexively.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: The capex-earnings loop depends on equity prices, so a market drop would reverse it; estimates are Karsan's own approximations.

insights.claim: US household equity holdings are at the highest share of wealth ever, above tech-bubble and COVID-recovery levels, with the spread to residential real estate the widest ever, so a sharp equity correction would transmit a larger negative wealth effect and financial conditions tightening, though a Fed response would act as a buffer.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann (Goldman Sachs)
insights.so_what: Economy is more equity-dependent than ever, raising the policy-put expectation and the damage from a drawdown.

insights.claim: Karsan likens today to 1999, when 27% earnings growth came from capex, and says the closed loop of markets driving the economy makes the system fragile and concentrated, though bubbles can persist for years and calling the top is nearly impossible.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Argues for owning convexity rather than shorting; Mueller-Glissmann counters the corporate sector looks less bubbly than 1999.

themes.theme: Debt refinancing, supply and bond-market structure

insights.claim: Karsan argues bonds work with long and variable lags because debt was financed near 0% in 2021 with 5-8 year durations, so the pain arrives as it is rolled at much higher rates, coinciding with surging new issuance that crowds out the long end.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: The refinancing wall and supply wave keep upward pressure on long yields even after interventions like stablecoin rules, SLR changes and buybacks.

insights.claim: The structural cycle is a fight between innovation and inflation: innovation raises long-term real yields and crowds out bond demand near term, while higher inflation volatility and fiscal concerns make long-duration bonds structurally less friendly.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann (Goldman Sachs)
insights.so_what: Term premium should stay higher than in the pre-COVID era.

insights.claim: The 300-year average US 10-year yield is about 4.7% (about 4.5% excluding the 1970s) versus current yields of around 5.3-5.4%, so the question is whether the spread over the long-run average is fair compensation for the new regime.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann (Goldman Sachs)
insights.so_what: Current yields are above historical averages but not obviously excessive given inflation and fiscal risk.
insights.quote: If you look at the 300ear average of the US 10ear yield, it's uh 4.7.

insights.claim: Hyperscaler debt financing means continued earnings growth requires more borrowing, which crowds out the long end further, a potential circular loop; hyperscaler CDS are breaking out and the MOVE index is rising while the VIX stays calm.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Credit and rates volatility are signaling stress that equity volatility has not priced.
insights.quote: CDS are starting to break out

insights.claim: Equity volatility looks cheap versus credit spreads, rates volatility and commodity volatility, and Goldman leans toward upside convexity being cheap into year-end, favouring slightly longer-dated calls to run equity exposure including in tech.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann (Goldman Sachs)
insights.so_what: Express bullish or hedged views via long-dated calls rather than outright shorts.

insights.claim: Single-stock volatility in hyperscalers reset lower after the summer momentum unwind, making longer-dated tech calls cheaper than before.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann (Goldman Sachs)
insights.so_what: Cheaper tech optionality than earlier in the year.

insights.claim: Index volatility is low because dispersion is high: nearly 40% of S&P 500 stocks had a negative beta to the index over three months (20-25% over one year), unprecedented since the tech bubble, mostly rate-sensitive, bond-proxy, low-volatility and high-dividend stocks.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann (Goldman Sachs)
insights.so_what: Index-level calm masks large divergence; the laggards could be the diversifier if AI unwinds.

insights.claim: Karsan argues structural index volatility selling (structured products, carry) pins the index and forces dispersion, pushing momentum and concentrating gains in capex beneficiaries, and that dispersion has risen almost one-for-one with index vol selling since 2017; Mueller-Glissmann sees a chicken-and-egg with fundamental earnings dispersion.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Vol suppression and dispersion are mutually reinforcing and make the system prone to extreme outcomes when direction reverses.

insights.claim: Clients show more interest in dispersion carry because index implied correlation and dispersion are extreme.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann (Goldman Sachs)
insights.so_what: Crowding in dispersion trades is a risk to monitor.

insights.claim: During the tech bubble the Nasdaq fell 80% and the S&P 500 46%, while simple defensive baskets such as S&P dividend aristocrats or a low-vol ETF finished up about 10%, so rotation into lagging defensives is a proven diversifier.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann (Goldman Sachs)
insights.so_what: Negative-beta laggards can hedge AI-concentration risk.
insights.quote: the market was down 46%, NASDAQ down 80

insights.claim: An asset allocator's two value-adds are market timing and diversification; since timing a bubble peak is very hard (calling it in 1998 was two years early), the right response is risk management: factor diversification, bonds in the belly rather than long duration, and equity volatility as an asset class.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann (Goldman Sachs)
insights.so_what: Prepare rather than predict; use options and diversifiers.

insights.claim: Karsan notes that in 1998-2000 the easiest trade was owning out-of-the-money calls or longer-dated cheap volatility instead of stocks, and that bubbles tend to trade in megaphone patterns.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Supports owning cheap long-dated convexity over shorting in a late-stage boom.

insights.claim: FX volatility also looks remarkably cheap given recent violent convex moves in the euro, Swiss franc and yen, and FX vol expressions could protect non-home-currency assets.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann (Goldman Sachs)
insights.so_what: FX is no longer boring or mean-reverting; options on currencies are an attractive hedge.

insights.claim: Asset owners are moving toward real assets, more home bias because of FX risk, and gold; gold's convexity arises when there is a trust problem (1970s central banks, GFC financial system, post-COVID governments), and Goldman is constructive on gold as a geopolitical diversifier.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann (Goldman Sachs)
insights.so_what: Policy-driven volatility generates inflation and distrust, supporting real assets and gold.
insights.quote: gold has this very interesting convexity when there is an issue with trust

insights.claim: Bonds are becoming a less reliable partner for equities because fiscal concerns, policy uncertainty and political volatility are widespread, unlike the deflation and austerity era in which bonds were a good buffer.
insights.speaker: Christian Mueller-Glissmann (Goldman Sachs)
insights.so_what: Duration is a weaker hedge; rely more on real assets, gold and vol.

insights.claim: Karsan predicts debasement is no longer years away but coming within the next year, a dramatically convex outcome for global markets, with the next crisis met by massive QE plus a cap on the long end, driving a structural inflation loop.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Positioning for debasement means owning real assets and leverage; he cites Hank Pollson's 'coming Treasury crisis'. Timing is Karsan's own view and not endorsed by the guest.
insights.quote: debasement that people have been talking about for some time is not is no longer two 5 10 years away it's coming in the next year

insights.claim: Karsan expects direct government investment in corporations via a sovereign wealth fund and Trump accounts at scale, with the government effectively printing money to buy stocks as Japan did for 15 years, extending the capex bubble beyond free-market funding.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Government equity support could sustain asset prices while debasing the currency; low-consensus, speculative.

insights.claim: Karsan's allocation: own gold, farmland and keep debt on real estate, since being under-levered may be the greatest risk in a debasement.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: Mirror the government's position of being long hard assets and short nominal debt.

insights.claim: A study of the 1960s-70s found FX, bond and gold volatility outperformed any other period while industrial commodities and equities underperformed, with equities going nowhere in nominal terms from 1968 to 1982 due to margin compression and discount-rate rises.
insights.speaker: Cem Karsan
insights.so_what: A possible analog for flat nominal equities despite inflation.
